title: Near-field Dressing of Thermal Emission
authors: Victor Guillemot, Raphael Mol, Riccardo Messina, Valentina Krachmalnicoff, Philippe Ben-Abdallah, Wilfrid Poirier, Yannick De Wilde
abstract: Radiative heat transfer at subwavelength distances is generally understood as enhanced energy exchange mediated by photon tunnelling between neighboring bodies. While near-field interactions can dramatically increase mutual heat transfer, whether they also modify the thermal radiation emitted by the bodies themselves remains an open question. Here we experimentally show that near-field electromagnetic coupling reshapes far-field thermal emission through a distance-dependent dressed emissivity. Using a dual-probe calorimetric platform, we independently monitor the radiative balance of two borosilicate microspheres over separations ranging from 120 micrometers to a few hundred nanometers, spanning the transition from the far field to the near field. Nanowatt-resolved differential radiometry reveals asymmetric heat fluxes and a non-monotonic response of the hotter sphere, demonstrating that thermal radiation is governed not only by emitter-bath interactions but also by coupling to the surrounding photonic environment. By analyzing the total power exchanged between the coupled system and the external thermal bath, we directly extract a dressed emissivity and show that near-field interactions renormalize the far-field thermal emission of the pair through a redistribution of the electromagnetic modes available to thermal fluctuations. These observations provide direct experimental evidence that thermal emitters are dressed by their electromagnetic environment, establishing a thermal analogue of the Purcell effect.
summary: This paper experimentally and theoretically proves that near-field electromagnetic coupling between objects alters their far-field thermal emission. By measuring the radiative balance of two microspheres across varying separations, the authors quantify a 'dressed emissivity.' This finding establishes a measurable thermal analogue to the Purcell effect, showing that the surrounding photonic environment dictates the emitted radiation spectrum.
main_problem: The study investigates whether near-field electromagnetic coupling between two bodies modifies their far-field thermal radiation, moving beyond simply quantifying the enhanced energy exchange between neighbors.
main_result: The authors experimentally and theoretically demonstrate that near-field interactions renormalize the far-field thermal emission by inducing a distance-dependent 'dressed emissivity,' establishing a thermal analogue of the Purcell effect.
method: The work combines high-precision differential calorimetry experiments with advanced theoretical modeling using fluctuational electrodynamics (e.g., SCUFF-EM solvers).
model_or_system: The system consists of two borosilicate microspheres placed in a vacuum chamber, allowing for controlled separation distances spanning from the far field ($\gg \lambda$) down to the near field ($d \sim 100$ nm).
key_observables: Asymmetric heat fluxes, non-monotonic temperature responses, and the extracted distance-dependent dressed emissivity ($\Delta\epsilon_{	ext{dress}}(d)$).
important_parameters: Separation distance ($d$), which is varied from $120 \mu	ext{m}$ down to hundreds of nanometers; the thermal wavelength ($\lambda_{Wien}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on decomposing total radiative power into sphere-bath, sphere-sphere, and external bath components. Semi-analytical models are limited when $d$ approaches $\lambda_{Wien}$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup (dual-probe platform), temperature variations showing asymmetry vs. separation, and comparisons between full-wave simulations (SCUFF-EM) and semi-analytical predictions for heat flux and dressed emissivity.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem by noting the gap in understanding near-field effects on emitted radiation. It details the experimental platform and measurement techniques to quantify radiative balance, develops theoretical frameworks using fluctuational electrodynamics, and presents results showing spectral renormalization via the dressed emissivity.
why_interesting: This work provides a direct, measurable thermal analogue of the Purcell effect, demonstrating how coupling to an electromagnetic environment modifies fundamental radiation properties (emissivity) in nanoscale systems, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and open system dynamics.
